newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia industry tips rise in strike action.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia industry tips rise in strike action.

text.p: Australian manufacturers expect industrial action to rise over the next few months as some of the nation's most powerful trade unions use their muscle to push for annual wage rises of over five percent from employers.

"I am sure we are going to find that the incidence of industrial action is going to increase over the next few months," Metal Trades Industry Association (MTIA) official Roger Boland told Reuters on Thursday.

The MTIA, which represents major firms in the manufacturing and engineering and construction industries, is bracing for a major showdown with workers after a key union recently won a 16 percent pay rise over three years at a Melbourne glass factory.

The pay rise, agreed to by industrial conglomerate BTR Nylex Ltd after a protracted and sometimes violent dispute with maintenance workers at the factory, is being seen as a new benchmark for manufacturing unions, a union official said.
"It could become a benchmark, yes," said Vince Theuma, Victoria state organiser for the Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union (AMWU) which negotiated the BTR wage rise.

"This dispute has been a high-profile dispute, so all the working people of Australia have heard about this dispute....I have no doubt that the expectation of our members is that they don't do any worse than this particular deal," he said.

The MTIA's Boland agreed that other big unions, including the Australian Workers' Union and Communication and Electrical and Plumbing Union, would try to match the wage rises when they sat down with employers over the next six months.
Around six or seven of Australia's 20 biggest manufacturers are preparing to sit down with unions to renegotiate wage deals, known as enterprise agreements, due to expire by March.
"Employers are not going to be a pushover this time around and are going to resist excessive demands," Boland said.
"As a general proposition employers should be looking at enterprise outcomes in the order of three to four percent per annum over the next couple of years and no more," he added.
Boland said he feared the BTR dispute, during which police on horseback baton-charged a picket line outside the factory, could set the tone for the impending round of wage negotiations.

He declined to name any of the companies due to renegotiate their wages bill, but the AMWU's Theuma said about six or seven enterprise agreements were due to expire at BTR sites around the country by the end of calendar 1996.

Boland described the BTR dispute here as "peculiar to that site" and said the 16 percent wage rise was offset by the AMWU's agreement to major changes in work practices which were likely to be ignored in the other wage negotiations.

Employers will meet next month to discuss their position, he said. "It is with a view to dampening down wage expectations and...make it clear that unless they are going to get productivity offsets wage increases of the order of five or six percents are excessive," Boland said.
Wages growth is a major concern for the Reserve Bank of Australia in deciding the direction of the next move in official interest rates.
Official data show average weekly ordinary-time earnings rose 4.4 percent year-on-year in the May quarter, just outside the central bank's comfort zone.

The Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU), which says workers are driving a harder bargain after the scrapping of the previous government's labour accord, on Wednesday succeeded in persuading the national industrial tribunal to hear its "living wage" claim.

The claim, which seeks improvements to minimum rates of pay of up to 8.75 percent, will be heard in December. The ACTU has quoted government officials as saying the ACTU claim would increase Australia's total wages bill by two percent.
